passage_text: Researchers investigated the effect of a novel dietary supplement on glucose tolerance in adult mice. Twenty-four male C57BL/6 mice were randomly assigned to one of four groups: (1) control diet, (2) control diet plus placebo, (3) high‑fat diet, and (4) high‑fat diet plus supplement. The study lasted 12 weeks, during which weekly blood glucose levels were measured following an intraperitoneal glucose tolerance test. At the end of the trial, the researchers recorded the area under the curve (AUC) for each mouse and compared the mean AUC of the groups. The data suggested that the high‑fat + supplement group had a lower mean AUC than the high‑fat group. No group received the supplement on a control diet, so its effect in control‑diet mice was not tested. The authors concluded that the supplement may ameliorate diet‑induced glucose intolerance, though they noted the need for a larger sample size to confirm the effect.
stem: Based on the table, which conclusion is best supported by the data?

options.A: Mean AUC was lower in the high‑fat + supplement group than in the high‑fat group.
options.B: The supplement lowered AUC in mice fed the control diet.
options.C: Mean AUC in the high‑fat + supplement group was equal to that of the control group.
options.D: Mean AUC in the high‑fat group was lower than in the control group.

explanation: Correct: Mean AUC was 1550 in the high‑fat + supplement group versus 1900 in the high‑fat group, a lower value. Why the others are wrong: B) no group received the supplement on a control diet, so this cannot be concluded. C) 1550 differs from the control mean of 1200. D) the high‑fat mean (1900) is higher than the control mean (1200).
trap: Option B tempts readers to assume the supplement was tested in control‑diet mice, but the table has no such group.

stem: If the researchers wanted to test whether the supplement alone (without a high‑fat diet) improves glucose tolerance, which experimental design adjustment would be most appropriate?

options.A: Add a fifth group receiving the supplement on a control diet.
options.B: Increase the number of mice in each existing group to 12.
options.C: Replace the high‑fat diet with a low‑carbohydrate diet.
options.D: Administer the supplement to all mice regardless of diet.

explanation: Adding a group that receives the supplement on a control diet isolates the supplement’s effect independent of diet type.
trap: Option D would confound the supplement effect with diet, making it impossible to attribute changes to the supplement alone.

stem: Calculate the percent reduction in mean AUC for the high‑fat + supplement group relative to the high‑fat group.
explanation: Correct: B) (1900 - 1550)/1900 x 100 = 350/1900 x 100 = 18.4%. Why the others are wrong: A) 10.5% is far smaller than the 350-unit drop relative to 1900. C) 22.6% divides the 350-unit drop by the supplement mean (1550) instead of the high-fat reference (1900). D) 25.3% overstates the reduction and does not follow from the table values.
trap: Dividing the 350-unit drop by the high-fat + supplement mean (1550) instead of the high-fat reference mean (1900), which gives 22.6% instead of 18.4%.

stem: Which statement is NOT supported by the passage and table?

options.A: The supplement would lower AUC to the same degree in mice fed a control diet.
options.B: Mean AUC in the control + placebo group (1180) was close to that of the control group (1200).
options.C: The authors noted that a larger sample size would be needed to confirm the effect.
options.D: Mean AUC in the high-fat group was higher than in the control group.

explanation: Correct: A) The supplement was never given to control-diet mice, so the study cannot show that its effect would be the same on a control diet. Why the others are wrong: B) 1180 and 1200 are close, so this describes the table. C) The passage says the authors noted the need for a larger sample. D) 1900 is higher than 1200.
trap: Treating the supplement benefit seen on the high-fat diet as if it applied to every diet, although no control-diet mice received the supplement.

stem: Which conclusion is best supported by the study's design and data?

options.A: In these mice, the supplement lowered mean AUC relative to the high-fat diet alone; its effect on a control diet was not tested.
options.B: The supplement is an effective treatment for glucose intolerance in people.
options.C: The supplement has no effect on glucose tolerance.
options.D: The supplement lowers AUC in mice regardless of diet.

explanation: Correct: A) The high-fat + supplement mean (1550) was below the high-fat mean (1900), but no control-diet mice received the supplement. Why the others are wrong: B) The study used mice only, so human effectiveness is not shown. C) AUC was lower with the supplement, so 'no effect' contradicts the table. D) Only the high-fat diet was tested with the supplement, so effects on other diets are unknown.
trap: Extrapolating from one mouse study on a high-fat diet to humans or to all diets, when the data cover only mice fed a high-fat diet.
